title: Book 12
paragraphs: Lord, my heart is stirred by the words of your holy scripture, and it stays busy with them, for all the poverty of my life. And this is usually how it goes: the poverty of human understanding is rich in words, because asking a question takes more saying than finding an answer, and requesting takes longer than receiving, and the hand that knocks has more work to do than the hand that receives. We hold your promise — who can annul it? If God is for us, who can be against us? Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. These are your own promises — and who needs to fear being deceived, when it is the Truth that promises?

The lowliness of my tongue confesses to your greatness that you made heaven and earth — this heaven I see, and this earth I walk on, the earth from which comes the flesh I carry about; you made it. But where, Lord, is that heaven of heavens we hear of in the words of the Psalm: "The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men"? Where is that heaven we do not see, in comparison to which all this that we do see is only earth? For this whole physical universe, not being wholly present everywhere at once, has received its share of beauty in these lower regions, the lowest of which is our earth; but compared to that heaven of heavens, even the heaven that belongs to our earth is merely earth. Indeed, both these great bodies might not unreasonably be called earth next to that unknown heaven, which belongs to the Lord, not to the sons of men.

Now this earth was invisible and without form, and there was some depth of abyss I cannot name, over which there was no light, because it had no shape. So you had it written that darkness lay upon the face of the deep — and what is that but the absence of light? For if there had been light, where would it have been except spread over everything, above, shining? Where light was absent, then, what was the presence of darkness but the absence of light? Darkness lay upon it, then, because light was not upon it — just as where there is no sound, there is silence. And what is it to have silence there but to have no sound there? Have you not, Lord, taught this to the soul that confesses to you? Have you not taught me, Lord, that before you gave form and variety to this formless matter, there was nothing — no color, no shape, no body, no spirit? And yet not utterly nothing, for there was a certain formlessness, without any beauty.

How then should it be named, so that it could be conveyed, at least to some degree, to slower minds, except by some ordinary word? And of all the parts of the world, what comes nearer to sheer formlessness than earth and the deep? For occupying the lowest level, they are less beautiful than the higher parts, which are all transparent and shining. So why should I not think that the formlessness of matter — which you created without beauty, in order to make this beautiful world out of it — is fittingly suggested to us by the name "earth invisible and without form."

So when the mind looks for what the senses might grasp in this, and says to itself, "It is no intelligible form, like life or justice, because it is the raw material of bodies; nor is it an object of sense, because, being invisible and without form, there was in it nothing to see or sense" — while the human mind says this to itself, it may try either to know this thing by being ignorant of it, or to be ignorant of it by knowing it.

But if I wanted to confess to you the whole of it, with my voice and my pen — whatever you yourself taught me about that matter — here is how it went. I had heard the name before without understanding it, and when people who did not understand it either told me about it, I imagined it as having countless different shapes, and so did not really conceive of it at all. My mind tossed about foul and monstrous "shapes," pulled out of all order — shapes all the same — and I called this "without form" not because it lacked all form, but because it had a form of the kind my mind, if it were shown to it, would turn away from as strange and jarring, the kind that would trouble our human frailty. And even so, what I was imagining was "without form" not in the sense of being deprived of all form, but only in comparison with more beautiful forms. True reasoning persuaded me that I had to strip away every last remnant of form whatsoever if I wanted to conceive of matter as absolutely without form — and I could not do it. I could sooner imagine that a thing deprived of all form did not exist at all than conceive of something in between form and nothing — neither formed nor nothing, a formless almost-nothing. So my mind stopped questioning my spirit on this point, since my spirit was full of the images of formed bodies, changing and varying them as it pleased. I turned instead to the bodies themselves, and looked more closely into their changeableness, by which they stop being what they were and begin to be what they were not; and I suspected that this very shifting from form to form happened by way of some formless condition, not through sheer nothing — yet this I wanted to know, not merely to suspect. If I tried to confess to you the whole of it, with voice and pen, every knot you undid for me in this question, what reader would hold out to take it all in? Even so my heart will not stop giving you honor and a song of praise for the things it is unable to put into words. For the changeableness of changeable things is itself capable of taking on all those forms into which changeable things are changed. And this changeableness — what is it? Is it soul? Is it body? Is it whatever it is that makes up soul or body? If one could say "a nothing-something," an "it-is, it-is-not," I would say: this was it. And yet in some way it already existed even then, in that it was capable of receiving these visible, composite shapes.

But where did it get even this degree of being, except from you, from whom all things come, insofar as they are at all? And yet the more unlike you a thing is, the further it is from you — though this is not a distance of place. You, then, Lord, who are not one thing in one place and something else in another, but always the very same, the very same, the very same — Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty — in the Beginning, which comes from you, by your Wisdom, born of your own substance, created something, and created it out of nothing. For you created heaven and earth — not out of yourself, since then they would have been equal to your only-begotten Son, and through him equal to you as well; and it would in no way have been right for anything not of you to be equal to you. And there was nothing else besides you out of which you could have made them, O God, one Trinity and three-fold Unity; and so out of nothing did you create heaven and earth, a great thing and a small thing, for you are almighty and good, and make all things good — even the great heaven and the small earth. You existed, and there was nothing else, out of which you created heaven and earth: things of two kinds, one near to you, the other near to nothing; one to which you alone should be superior, the other to which nothing should be inferior.

But that heaven of heavens was for you alone, Lord; while the earth you gave to the sons of men, to see and touch, was not the earth as we now see and touch it. For it was invisible, without form, and there was a deep over which there was no light — or rather, darkness lay above the deep, meaning more than merely "in" the deep. Because this deep of waters, visible now, even at its depths has a light suited to its nature, perceptible in some degree to the fish and the creeping things at its bottom. But that whole first deep was almost nothing, because up to that point it was entirely without form — yet there was already something there that could be given form. For you, Lord, made the world out of formless matter, which you made out of nothing, next to nothing, in order to make from it those great things we sons of men marvel at. For this physical heaven is a very marvel — the firmament between water and water, which, on the second day, after the creation of light, you said, "Let it be made," and it was made. This firmament you called heaven — the heaven, that is, belonging to this earth and sea, which you made on the third day, by giving a visible shape to the formless matter you had made before all days. For already, before all days, you had made a heaven — but that was the heaven of this heaven, because in the beginning you had made heaven and earth. But this same earth you made was formless matter, because it was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep — and out of this invisible and formless earth, this formlessness, this almost-nothing, you were able to make all these things of which this changeable world is made up, though it does not itself remain fixed; and its very changeableness shows itself in the fact that times can be observed and counted in it. For times come about through the alteration of things, while the shapes — whose matter is the invisible earth just mentioned — are varied and turned.

And this is why the Spirit, your servant's teacher, when it tells us that you created heaven and earth in the Beginning, says nothing about times, nothing about days. For truly that heaven of heavens which you created in the Beginning is some intellectual creature which, although in no way coeternal with you, the Trinity, still shares in your eternity, and through the sweetness of that most blessed contemplation of you, holds its own changeableness strongly in check; and, without any falling away since its first creation, clinging close to you, it is set beyond all the turning cycle of times. Nor, indeed, is this same formlessness of the earth — invisible and without form — counted among the days. For where there is no shape and no order, nothing comes and nothing goes; and where that is absent, there plainly are no days, nor any succession of stretches of time.

Let the Light speak to me — the Truth, the Light of my heart — not my own darkness. I fell away into that darkness and became darkened; but even from there, even from there, I loved you. I went astray, and I remembered you. I heard your voice behind me, calling me to return, and I barely heard it through the uproar of the enemies of peace. And now, look, I return in distress, panting after your fountain. Let no one stop me! I will drink of it, and so live. Let me not be my own life; left to myself I lived badly, I was death to myself, and I come back to life in you. Speak to me, talk with me. I have believed your Books, and their words are full of deep mystery.

You have already told me, Lord, in a strong voice, in my inner ear, that you are eternal, the only one who has immortality, since you cannot be changed in shape or in motion, nor is your will altered by times — for no will that varies is immortal. This is clear to me in your sight, and I beg you, let it become clearer and clearer to me still; and in that unfolding clarity, let me soberly remain under your wings. You have also told me, Lord, in a strong voice, in my inner ear, that you have made all natures and substances that are not what you yourself are, and yet exist; and that only what does not exist is not from you, along with the movement of the will away from you, who are, toward that which exists in a lesser degree — because such a movement is transgression and sin; and that no one's sin either harms you or disturbs the order of your governance, from beginning to end. This is clear to me in your sight, and I beg you, let it become clearer and clearer to me still, and in that unfolding clarity, let me soberly remain under your wings.

You have also told me, in a strong voice, in my inner ear, that this creature too is not coeternal with you — the creature whose only happiness is you, and which, with a purity that never wavers, drawing its nourishment from you, never at any place or time puts forth its natural changeableness; and, since you are always present to it, to whom it holds itself with its whole affection, having no future to look forward to and carrying nothing remembered forward into a past, it is neither altered by any change nor pulled apart into any times. Blessed creature, if such a thing exists, for clinging to your Blessedness — blessed in you, its eternal Indweller and its Enlightener! Nor can I find any better name for the heaven of heavens which is the Lord's than "your house," which contemplates your delights without ever straying off toward anything else — one pure mind, harmoniously one, held in that settled peace of holy spirits, citizens of your city in the heavenly places, far above these heavenly places we see.

By this the soul whose pilgrimage has grown long and far from home may understand — if she now thirsts for you, if her tears have now become her bread, while day after day they say to her, "Where is your God?" — if she now seeks one thing from you and desires it, that she may dwell in your house all the days of her life (and what is her life but you? and what are your days but your eternity, like your years that do not fail, because you are always the same?) — by this, then, may the soul that is able understand how far above all times you are, eternal; seeing that your house, which never went off into a distant country, though it is not coeternal with you, yet by clinging to you continually and unfailingly suffers no changeableness of times. This is clear to me in your sight, and I beg you, let it become clearer and clearer to me still, and in that unfolding clarity, let me soberly remain under your wings.

There is, look, some formlessness or other I cannot name in these changes among the last and lowest of your creatures; and who will tell me (unless it is someone who, out of the emptiness of his own heart, wanders and tosses himself about among his own fancies?) — who but such a person would tell me that, if every shape were so worn away and consumed that nothing remained but that formlessness through which the thing was changed and turned from one shape into another, that formlessness by itself could display the successive changes of times? For plainly it could not, because without a variety of movements there are no times, and there is no variety where there is no shape.

Considering these things, as much as you grant me, my God, as much as you rouse me to knock, and as much as you open to me when I knock, I find two things that you made outside the reach of time, neither of them coeternal with you. One is so formed that, without any break in contemplation, without any interval of change — though changeable, it is not in fact changed — it may fully enjoy your eternity and unchangeableness. The other was so formless that it did not even have what could be changed from one form to another, whether of motion or of rest, so as to become subject to time. But this you did not leave in that formless state, because before all days, in the Beginning, you created Heaven and Earth — the two things I have been speaking of. "But the Earth was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep." In these words the formlessness is conveyed to us, so that minds unable to conceive an utter absence of all form, without lapsing into thinking of nothing at all, may be drawn along by degrees — out of which another Heaven might be created, together with a visible, well-formed earth, and the waters set in their various order, and whatever else belongs to the shaping of the world, recorded as having been created not without days; and created, moreover, as being of such a nature that the successive changes of times could take place within them, being subject to the appointed alterations of motions and of forms.

This, then, is what I take it to mean, my God, when I hear your Scripture say, "In the beginning God made Heaven and Earth: and the Earth was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep," without mentioning on what day you created them; this is what I take it to mean — that on account of the Heaven of heavens, that intellectual Heaven whose intelligences know everything at once, not in part, not dimly, not as through a mirror, but as a whole, openly, face to face — not this thing now and that thing later, but, as I said, knowing everything at once, without any succession of times — and on account of the earth invisible and without form, likewise without any succession of times (a succession that brings with it "this thing now, that thing later"; because where there is no form, there is no distinction between things) — it is on account of these two, then, one primordially formed and one primordially formless — the one, heaven, but the Heaven of heaven; the other, earth, but earth invisible and without form — it is on account of these two, I take it, that your Scripture, without mentioning days, said, "In the Beginning God created Heaven and Earth." For it immediately went on to specify which earth it meant; and also, since the Firmament is recorded as created on the second day and called Heaven, this tells us which Heaven it had spoken of earlier, without mentioning days.

What a wondrous depth your words have! Their surface, look, lies open before us, inviting to little ones — and yet what a wondrous depth they are! O my God, what a wondrous depth! It is an awe-filled thing to look into it — an awe that is honor, and a trembling that is love. Its enemies I hate fiercely; I wish you would slay them with your two-edged sword, so that they might no longer be its enemies — for I love, in this way, to have them slain to themselves, so that they may live to you. But look, there are others too, not fault-finders but praisers of the book of Genesis: "The Spirit of God," they say, "who through his servant Moses wrote these things, would not have wanted those words understood this way; he would not have wanted them understood as you say, but differently, as we say." To these, with you yourself, O God of all, as judge, I answer as follows.

"Will you say that what Truth tells me in a strong voice in my inner ear is false — concerning the Creator's eternity, that his substance is in no way changed by time, nor his will separate from his substance? So he does not will one thing now and another later, but once, all at once, and forever, he wills everything he wills — not again and again, not now this, now that; nor does he will afterward what he did not will before, nor fail to will what he willed before; because a will like that would be changeable, and no changeable thing is eternal — but our God is eternal. Again, what he tells me in my inner ear: the expectation of things to come becomes sight when they arrive, and that same sight becomes memory once they have passed. Now all thinking that shifts like this is changeable, and no changeable thing is eternal — but our God is eternal." These things I draw together and conclude, and I find that my God, the eternal God, has not made any creature by any new act of will, nor does his knowledge admit of anything passing away. "What will you say to this, then, you who argue against it? Are these things false?" "No," they say. "What then? Is it false that every nature already formed, or matter capable of taking form, exists only because it comes from him who is supremely good, because he supremely is?" "We do not deny that either," they say. "What then? Do you deny that there is a certain sublime creature, clinging with so chaste a love to the true and truly eternal God, that although it is not coeternal with him, it is not torn away from him, nor dissolved into the variety and succession of times, but rests in the truest contemplation of him alone?" Because you, O God, show yourself to the one who loves you as much as you command, and are enough for him, and so he does not turn away from you, nor toward himself. This is the house of God — not made of earthly stuff, nor of a heavenly mass that is physical, but spiritual, and a partaker of your eternity, because it never falls away, forever. For you have made it fast forever and ever; you have given it a law it shall not overstep. And yet it is not coeternal with you, O God, because it is not without a beginning — for it was made.

For although we find no time before it — since wisdom was created before all things, not that Wisdom which is entirely equal and coeternal with you, our God, its Father, and through whom all things were created, and in whom, as the Beginning, you created heaven and earth; but that wisdom which is itself created, that is, the intellectual nature which, by contemplating the light, is itself light. For this nature, though created, is also called wisdom. But the difference between the Light that gives light and the light that is given light is the same as the difference between the Wisdom that creates and the wisdom that is created — as between the Righteousness that justifies and the righteousness that comes into being through justification. For we too are called your righteousness, as a certain servant of yours says, "that we might become the righteousness of God in him." So, since a certain created wisdom was created before all things — the rational and intellectual mind of that chaste city of yours, our mother above, which is free and eternal in the heavens (in what heavens, if not in those that praise you, the Heaven of heavens? Because this too is the Heaven of heavens that belongs to the Lord) — though we find no time before it, since whatever has been created before all things also comes before the creature of time, still the Eternity of the Creator himself comes before it, from whom, being created, it took its beginning — not a beginning in time, for time itself did not yet exist, but a beginning of its creation.

So it is, in relation to you, our God, entirely other than you, and not the very same as you — because though we find time neither before it nor even in it (since it is fitting for it always to behold your face, and it is never drawn away from that gaze, and so it is not altered by any change), there is nevertheless in it a capacity for change, by which it would grow dark and cold, were it not that, by a strong affection clinging to you, like an unending noon, it shines and glows because of you. O house most full of light and delight! I have loved your beauty, and the place where the glory of my Lord dwells, your builder and owner. Let my wayfaring sigh after you, and let me say to him who made you: let him take possession of me too, within you, since he made me as well. I have wandered off like a lost sheep; but on the shoulders of my Shepherd, your builder, I hope to be carried back to you.

"What do you say to this, you objectors I have been speaking to, who nevertheless believe Moses to have been the holy servant of God, and his books the oracles of the Holy Spirit? Is this not the house of God — not coeternal with God, indeed, but eternal after its own measure, in the heavens — when you search for changes of time in it in vain, because you will not find any? For that which always finds it good to cling fast to God surpasses all extension and all the revolving periods of time." "It is," they say. "What then, of everything my heart cried out loudly to my God, when it inwardly heard the voice of his praise — which part of it do you claim to be false? Is it that the matter was without form, and that, because there was no form in it, there was no order? But where there was no order, there could be no succession of times; and yet this almost nothing, inasmuch as it was not altogether nothing, certainly came from him from whom comes whatever exists, to whatever degree it exists." "That too," they say, "we do not deny."

With these people I now debate a little in your presence, my God — people who grant all these things to be true, which your Truth whispers to my soul. As for those who deny them, let them bark and deafen themselves all they like; I will try to talk them into quiet, and to open in them a way for your word. But if they refuse me and push me away, I beg you, my God, do not be silent to me. Speak truly in my heart, for only you speak that way; and I will leave them alone, blowing dust outside and raising it into their own eyes, while I myself go into my inner room and sing there a song of love to you, groaning with groans that cannot be uttered, on my wayfaring journey, remembering Jerusalem, with my heart lifted up toward her — Jerusalem my homeland, Jerusalem my mother, and you who rule over her, the Enlightener, Father, Guardian, Husband, the pure and strong delight, the solid joy, and every unspeakable good thing, all at once, because you are the one sovereign and true Good. Nor will I be turned aside, until you gather everything I am, out of this scattered and disordered state, into the peace of that most dear mother of ours, where the firstfruits of my spirit already are (which is how I am assured of these things), and you shape and confirm the rest forever, my God, my Mercy. But as for those who do not claim all these truths to be false, who honor your holy Scripture, set forth by holy Moses, placing it, as we do, at the very summit of authority to be followed, and yet contradict me on some point — to them I answer this: let you yourself judge, our God, between my confessions and these men's contradictions.

For they say, "Though these things are true, still Moses did not mean those two things when, by revelation of the Spirit, he said, In the beginning God created heaven and earth. He did not mean, by the name heaven, that spiritual or intellectual creature that always beholds the face of God; nor, by the name earth, that formless matter." "What then?" "That man of God," they say, "meant what we say — this is what he declared by those words." "What?" "By the name heaven and earth," they say, "he meant first to signify, broadly and in summary, this whole visible world — so that afterward, by listing the several days, he could set out in detail, piece by piece, all the things it pleased the Holy Spirit to state this way. For the people he was speaking to were so unrefined and carnal that he judged them fit to be entrusted only with knowledge of God's works that were visible." They agree, however, that under the words "earth invisible and without form," and "that dark deep" (out of which it is later shown that all these visible things we all know were made and arranged during those "days"), it is not unreasonable to understand this formless first matter.

But what if someone else says that "this same formlessness and confusion of matter was conveyed first of all under the name heaven and earth, precisely because out of it came this visible world, with all the beings that plainly appear in it — a world that is often itself called by the name heaven and earth, once created and completed?" And what if yet another says that "invisible and visible nature is indeed not inappropriately called heaven and earth, and so the whole of creation, which God made in his Wisdom — that is, in the Beginning — was summed up under those two words? Even so, since all things are made not out of God's own substance but out of nothing (because they are not what God is, and there is a mutable nature in all of them, whether they remain fixed, as does the eternal house of God, or undergo change, as the soul and body of man do), the common matter of all things, visible and invisible — as yet unformed, though capable of form — out of which both heaven and earth were to be created (that is, the invisible and visible creature, once formed), was given the same names as the earth invisible and without form and the darkness upon the deep. But with this distinction: by the earth invisible and without form is meant bodily matter, prior to being given any form; and by the darkness upon the deep, spiritual matter, before it underwent any check on its unlimited fluidity, or received any light from Wisdom?"

There remains, too, the option for someone to say, if he wishes, that "the already perfected and formed natures, visible and invisible, are not what is meant by the name heaven and earth when we read, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, but that the as-yet unformed beginning of things, the stuff fit to receive form and making, was called by these names — because within it were confusedly contained, not yet distinguished by their qualities and forms, all those things which, now sorted into order, are called Heaven and Earth, the one the spiritual creation, the other the bodily one."

Having heard and carefully weighed all these views, I will not fight over words, for that does nothing but wear down the hearers. But the law is good, if a person uses it lawfully, for its purpose is love, out of a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. And our Master well knew which two commandments he hung the whole Law and the Prophets on. So what harm does it do me, my God, light of my eyes in secret, as I zealously confess these things — since several different things may be understood by these words, and yet all of them true — what harm, I say, does it do me, if I think the writer meant something other than what someone else thinks he meant? All of us readers, after all, strive to trace out and understand the meaning of the one we read; and since we believe he is speaking the truth, we would not dare imagine that he said anything we ourselves know or think to be false. So then, while everyone tries to understand in the Holy Scriptures the very thing the writer understood, what harm is there if someone understands what you, the light of all minds that speak truly, show him to be true — even though the one he is reading did not understand this particular thing, since he too understood a truth, just not this truth?

For it is true, Lord, that you made heaven and earth; and it is true too that the Beginning is your Wisdom, in which you create everything; and true again that this visible world consists for the most part of heaven and earth, which briefly sum up all created and made natures. And it is true too that whatever is subject to change points us toward a certain lack of form, by which it receives a form, or is changed, or is turned. It is true that whatever so clings to the unchangeable Form that, though capable of change, it is never in fact changed, is not subject to any times. It is true that that formlessness which is almost nothing cannot be subject to the alteration of times. It is true that the thing a thing is made of may, by a certain way of speaking, be called by the name of the thing made from it — so that the formlessness out of which heaven and earth were made might itself be called heaven and earth. It is true that, among things having form, none comes nearer to having no form than the earth and the deep. It is true that you made not only every created and formed thing, but also whatever is capable of being created and formed — you, from whom all things come. It is true that whatever is formed out of what had no form was unformed before it was formed.

Out of these truths — which no one doubts, whose inner eye you have enabled to see such things, and who unwaveringly believes your servant Moses spoke in the Spirit of truth — out of all these, then, one person takes this reading, saying: "In the Beginning God made the heaven and the earth," meaning, "in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the intelligible and the sensible creature, the spiritual and the bodily." Another takes this one, saying, "In the Beginning God made heaven and earth," meaning, "in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the whole mass of this bodily world, together with all the visible and familiar creatures it contains." Another takes this one, saying, "In the Beginning God made heaven and earth," meaning, "in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the formless matter of creatures both spiritual and bodily." Another takes this one, saying, "In the Beginning God created heaven and earth," meaning, "in his Word, coeternal with himself, God created the formless matter of the bodily creature, in which heaven and earth lay as yet undivided — matter which, now distinguished and formed, we today see in the mass of this world." And another takes this one, saying, "In the Beginning God made heaven and earth," meaning, "at the very outset of creating and working, God made that formless matter, containing within itself, still undivided, both heaven and earth — out of which, once formed, they now stand apart and are visible, together with everything in them."

And as for the meaning of the words that follow, out of all those truths, one person chooses this reading of "But the earth was invisible, and without form, and darkness was upon the deep": namely, "that bodily thing which God made was as yet a formless matter of bodily things, without order, without light." Another takes this reading of "The earth was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep": "this whole, which is called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, out of which the bodily heaven and the bodily earth were to be made, with everything in them known to our bodily senses." Another takes this reading of "The earth was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep": "this whole, which is called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, out of which was to be made both that intelligible heaven, elsewhere called the Heaven of heavens, and the earth — that is, the whole bodily nature, under which name this bodily heaven too is included — in a word, out of which every visible and invisible creature was to be created." Another takes this reading of "The earth was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep": "Scripture did not call that formlessness by the name of heaven and earth; rather, this formlessness already existed, which it called the earth invisible and without form, and the darkness upon the deep, of which it had already said, that God had made heaven and earth — meaning the spiritual and bodily creature." Another takes this reading of "The earth was invisible and without form, and darkness was upon the deep": "there already existed a certain formless matter, of which Scripture had already said that God made heaven and earth — namely, the whole bodily mass of the world, divided into two great parts, upper and lower, with all the ordinary, familiar creatures in them."

Now suppose someone tried to argue against these last two opinions like this: "If you will not allow that this formlessness of matter seems to be meant by the name heaven and earth, then there was something God had not made, out of which to make heaven and earth — for Scripture nowhere tells us that God made this matter, unless we take it to be signified by the name heaven and earth, or by earth alone, in the statement, In the Beginning God made the heaven and earth; so that in what follows, and the earth was invisible and without form (even though it pleased him to call the formless matter this), we are meant to understand no other matter than the one God made, of which it was written above, God made heaven and earth." The defenders of either of those last two views, on hearing this, would answer: "We do not deny that this formless matter was indeed created by God — that God from whom all things come, and who is supremely good; for just as we say that what is created and formed is a greater good, so we admit that what is made merely capable of creation and form is a lesser good, but still a good. We do say, however, that Scripture has not recorded that God made this formlessness, just as it has not recorded many other things — the Cherubim, and Seraphim, and those the Apostle names distinctly: Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers. That God made all of these is perfectly plain. Or, if everything is included in the statement he made heaven and earth, then what shall we say of the waters, over which the Spirit of God moved? For if they are included under the word earth, how can formless matter be meant by that name earth, when we see the waters are so beautiful? Or if it is taken that way, then why is it written that the firmament was made out of that same formlessness and called heaven, while nothing is written of the waters being made? For the waters do not remain formless and invisible, since we see them flowing in so handsome a manner. But if they received that beauty when God said, Let the waters under the firmament be gathered together — so that this gathering together was itself their being given form — then what shall be said of the waters above the firmament? For neither would they, if formless, have deserved so honorable a place, nor is it written by what word they were given form. If, then, Genesis is silent about God's making of something that neither sound faith nor well-grounded understanding doubts that God did make, and if, moreover, no sober teaching would dare claim these waters to be coeternal with God merely because we find them mentioned in the book of Genesis without finding when they were created — then why, since truth instructs us to, should we not understand that this formless matter, which Scripture here calls the earth invisible and without form and the dark deep, was created by God out of nothing, and is therefore not coeternal with him, even though this history has left out when it was created?"

Having heard and taken in these things, then, as far as my limited capacity allows (which I confess to you, Lord, since you know it), I see two kinds of disagreement that can arise when something is reported in words by truthful witnesses: one about the truth of the things themselves, the other about what the reporter meant. For we ask, in one way, about the making of the created world, what is actually true; and in another way, what Moses, that excellent minister of your faith, wanted his reader and hearer to understand by those words. As for the first kind of disagreement, away with all those who imagine they know as true what is in fact false; and as for the second, away too with all those who imagine that Moses wrote things that are false. But let me be joined with you, Lord, in fellowship with those, and delight myself in you together with those who feed on your truth, in the breadth of charity — and let us approach the words of your book together, and seek your meaning in them through the meaning of your servant, by whose pen you dispensed them to us.

But which of us, among the many truths that occur to inquirers in these words, as they are understood differently, could discover that single meaning so as to be able to declare, "This is what Moses thought," and "This is what he wanted understood in that history," with the same confidence he would use to say, "This is true," whether or not Moses thought this or that? For look, my God, I, your servant, who in this book have vowed a sacrifice of confession to you, and pray that by your mercy I may pay my vows to you — can I, with the same confidence with which I affirm that in your unchangeable world you created all things visible and invisible, also affirm that Moses meant nothing other than this when he wrote, "In the Beginning God made heaven and earth"? No. Because I do not see into his mind that he was thinking of this when he wrote these things, the way I see it to be certain in your truth. For he might have had his thoughts on God's starting to create, when he said "In the beginning"; and by heaven and earth, in this place, he might have meant no formed and completed nature, whether spiritual or bodily, but both of them still only beginning and as yet formless. For I can see that whichever of these two had been said, it could have been said truly; but which of the two he had in mind in these words, I cannot see so clearly. Even so, whether it was one of these, or some other sense besides that I have not mentioned here, which this great man saw in his mind when he spoke these words, I have no doubt that he saw it truly, and put it aptly into words.

So let no one harass me by saying, "Moses did not think as you say, but as I say" — for if such a person asked me, "How do you know that Moses thought what you infer from his words?" I ought to take it well, and would answer perhaps as I have above, or at greater length if he were stubborn. But when he says, "Moses did not mean what you say, but what I say," while still not denying that what each of us says might both be true — then, my God, life of the poor, in whose heart there is no contradiction, pour a softening dew into my heart, so that I may bear patiently with people who say this to me — not because they have a divine spirit and have seen into your servant's heart what they claim, but because they are proud, not knowing Moses' actual opinion but loving their own — not because it is truth, but because it is theirs. Otherwise they would love another true opinion just as much, the way I love what they say when they say something true — not because it is theirs, but because it is true; and precisely on that ground, not theirs, because it is true. But if they love it because it is true, then it is both theirs and mine, since it belongs in common to all lovers of truth. But when they insist that Moses did not mean what I say, but what they say, this I neither like nor love — for even if it were so, their rashness would still belong not to knowledge but to sheer boldness, and its parent would be not insight but vanity. And this is why, Lord, your judgments are fearsome — since your truth belongs neither to me, nor to him, nor to anyone else in particular, but to all of us together, whom you publicly call to share in it, warning us fearsomely not to treat it as private property, lest we be deprived of it. For whoever claims as his own what you offer for the enjoyment of all, and wants what belongs to everyone to be his alone, is driven away from what is held in common into what is merely his own — that is, from truth into a lie. For whoever speaks a lie speaks out of what is his own.

Listen, O God, best of judges; Truth itself, listen to what I am about to say to this objector, listen, for I am speaking before you, and before my brothers, who use your law lawfully, for the goal of love; listen and see, if it pleases you, what I shall say to him. This is the brotherly, peaceful reply I give him: "If we both see as true what you say, and both see as true what I say, where, I pray you, do we see it? Not I in you, nor you in me, but both of us in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls." Since, then, we are not fighting over the very light of the Lord God, there is no reason to fight over the thoughts of our neighbor, which we cannot see the way the unchangeable Truth is seen: for even if Moses himself had appeared to us and said, "This is what I meant," we would still not see it directly — we would only believe it. Let us not, then, be puffed up, one against another, beyond what is written; let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and our neighbor as ourself. With a view to these two commandments of love, unless we believe that Moses meant, in those books, whatever he in fact meant, we make God a liar by imagining our fellow servant's mind to have been other than what God has taught us. See, then, how foolish it is, given such an abundance of perfectly true meanings that can be drawn from those words, to rashly insist on which one Moses chiefly meant, and, with harmful quarrels, to offend the very love for whose sake he said everything, whose words we are attempting to explain.

And yet I, my God — lifter of my lowliness, rest of my labor, you who hear my confessions and forgive my sins — since you command me to love my neighbor as myself, I cannot believe that you gave a lesser gift to Moses, your faithful servant, than I would wish or desire you to have given me, had I been born in his time, and had you set me in that office, so that through the service of my heart and tongue those books might be given out which, for so long afterward, were to benefit all nations, and, from such a height of authority, were to overcome every false and proud teaching throughout the whole world. I would truly have wished, had I then been Moses (for we all come from the same clay — and what is man, except that you are mindful of him?) — I would have wished, had I been then what he was, and had you charged me to write the book of Genesis, to be given such a power of expression and such a style that those who could not yet understand how God created would not reject the words as beyond their grasp, and those who had already attained understanding would find that whatever true opinion they had arrived at by thought was not left out of those few words of your servant; and that if another man, by the light of truth, discovered still another true opinion, that too would not fail to be discoverable in those very same words.

For just as a spring confined to a narrow space is more abundant, and can supply a flow for more streams over a wider area, than any single one of those streams which, after running a long distance, comes from that same spring — so the account given by that dispenser of yours, meant to benefit many who would go on to discuss it, overflows out of a narrow compass of language into streams of the clearest truth, from which each person may draw out for himself whatever truth he can on these matters, one this truth, another that one, through longer stretches of reasoning. For some, when they read or hear these words, imagine God as though he were a man, or some mass endowed with boundless power, who, by some new and sudden decision, created heaven and earth outside himself, as if at a certain distance — two great bodies, one above and one below, in which everything was to be contained. And when they hear, "God said, Let it be made, and it was made," they imagine words begun and ended, sounding in time and then passing away, after whose departure the thing commanded came into being — and whatever else along these lines their familiarity with the material world might suggest. In such people, still little ones and still carnal, while their weakness is carried along by this humble kind of speech, as though in a mother's lap, their faith is wholesomely built up, so that they hold it for certain that God made all the natures which their eye beholds around them in such wonderful variety. And if anyone, scorning these words as too simple, should in a proud weakness stretch himself beyond this sheltering nest, he will, alas, fall miserably. Have pity, Lord God, lest those who pass by trample the unfledged bird, and send your angel to put it back in the nest, so that it may live until it can fly.

But others, for whom these words are no longer a nest but deep shady fruit-groves, see the fruit hidden within them, fly around joyfully, and with cheerful song seek it out and pick it. For reading or hearing these words, they see that all times, past and future, are surpassed by your eternal and unshifting existence, and yet that there is no creature formed in time that is not of your making. Since your will is the very same thing that you are, you made all things not by any change of will, nor by a will that had not existed before, and these things did not come out of you, in your own likeness, which is the form of all things, but out of nothing — a formless unlikeness that was to be given form by your likeness (returning to your Unity, in keeping with the capacity appointed to each thing, so far as is given to it in its kind), and all of it could be made very good, whether things remain fixed around you, or, arranged in gradation, removed in time and place, make or undergo the beautiful shifting changes of the universe. These things they see, and they rejoice, to whatever small degree is possible here, in the light of your truth.

Another sets his mind on the statement, "In the Beginning God made heaven and earth," and sees in it Wisdom, the Beginning, because Wisdom also speaks to us. Another likewise sets his mind on the same words, and by "Beginning" understands the start of created things — "In the beginning He made" as if it meant, "He made first." And among those who understand "In the Beginning" to mean "In your Wisdom you created heaven and earth," one believes that the matter out of which heaven and earth were to be created is what is called heaven and earth there; another believes it is natures already formed and distinguished; another, one already-formed nature, a spiritual one, under the name Heaven, and the other formless, a bodily matter, under the name Earth. And those who, by the names heaven and earth, understand matter still formless, out of which heaven and earth were to be formed, do not all understand it in the same way either — one takes it to be the matter out of which both the intelligible and the sensible creature were to be brought to completion; another takes it to be only that out of which this sensible, bodily mass was to be made, containing in its vast womb these visible, ordinary natures. Nor do those who believe that the creatures already ordered and arranged are what is called heaven and earth here understand the same thing — one takes it to mean both the invisible and the visible, the other the visible alone, in which we see this luminous heaven and dark earth, with everything they contain.

But someone who understands "In the Beginning He made" as meaning nothing other than "He made first" can only truly understand heaven and earth as the matter of heaven and earth — that is, the universal intelligible and bodily creation. For if he wanted to understand by this the universe as already formed, it could rightly be asked of him, "If God made this first, what did he make afterward?" — and after the universe he will find nothing; and then, against his will, he must face another question: "How did God make this thing first, if there was nothing after it?" But when he says that God made matter first formless and then formed, there is nothing absurd in that, provided he is able to tell apart what comes before something by eternity, what by time, what by choice, and what by origin. By eternity, as God comes before all things; by time, as the flower comes before the fruit; by choice, as the fruit comes before the flower; by origin, as the sound comes before the tune. Of these four, the first and the last mentioned are understood only with great difficulty; the two in the middle, easily. For it is a rare and much too lofty vision to behold your Eternity, Lord, unchangeably making changeable things, and in that sense coming before them. And who, again, has understanding sharp enough to see without great effort how sound comes before tune — because a tune is a formed sound, and a thing not yet formed can exist, whereas a thing that does not exist at all cannot be formed. So the material comes before the thing made from it — not because the material makes the thing, since the material is itself something made; nor does it come before by an interval of time. For we do not first, at one point in time, utter formless sounds with no singing in them, and then afterward adapt or shape them into the form of a song, the way wood or silver is shaped into a chest or a vessel — for such materials really do precede, in time, the forms of the things made from them. But it is not so with singing; for the moment it is sung, its sound is heard — there is no formless sound existing first, which is only afterward shaped into a song. For each sound, as soon as it is made, passes away, and you cannot find anything left over to call back and arrange by art. So the song is bound up entirely in its sound, and that sound is its material. And this sound is indeed given form, so that it becomes a tune; and so, as I said, the material of the sound comes before the form of the tune — not before in the sense of having any power to make it a tune, for a sound is in no way the craftsman of the tune, but is something bodily, placed at the disposal of the soul that sings, out of which to make a tune. Nor does it come first in time, since it is given forth together with the tune; nor first in choice, since a sound is not better than a tune — a tune being not merely a sound but a beautiful sound. But it does come first in origin, because a tune does not receive form in order to become a sound, but a sound receives form in order to become a tune. By this example, let anyone who can, understand how the matter of things was made first, and called heaven and earth, because heaven and earth were made out of it. Yet it was not made first in time, because the forms of things are what give rise to time, and that matter was without form; but now it exists, in time, as an object of sense together with its form. And yet nothing can be said about that matter except as though it came first in time, when in fact, in worth, it comes last — since formed things are superior to formless ones — and it is itself preceded by the Eternity of the Creator, so that there might be, out of nothing, something from which something else could be created.

In this diversity of true opinions, let Truth herself bring about harmony. And may our God have mercy on us, so that we may use the law lawfully, aiming at the purpose of the commandment, which is pure love. If, on this point, someone demands of me, "Which of these was the meaning of your servant Moses," this would not be in the spirit of my Confessions if I did not confess to you, "I do not know" — and yet I know that those readings are true, apart from the carnal ones, about which I have said what seemed necessary. And even those hopeful little ones who think in that way have this benefit: the words of your Book do not frighten them off, delivering lofty things in a lowly manner, and, in few words, a rich meaning. And all of us who, I admit, see and put into words the truth delivered in those words, let us love one another, and together love you, our God, the fountain of truth, if it is truth we thirst for, and not empty things; yes, let us so honor this servant of yours, the dispenser of this Scripture, full of your Spirit, as to believe that, when by your revelation he wrote these things, he had in mind whichever of these readings chiefly excels the others, both in the light of truth it gives and in the fruitfulness of the good it does.

So when one person says, "Moses meant it my way," and another, "No, my way," I think I speak more reverently when I say, "Why not rather both ways, if both are true?" And if there is a third reading, or a fourth, indeed if anyone else sees some other truth in those words, why should he not be believed to have seen all of these truths — he through whom the one God tempered the holy Scriptures to the understanding of many people, who were meant to see in them things true but various? For I myself — and I say this fearlessly, from my heart — if I were writing something meant to carry supreme authority, I would rather write it so that whatever truth anyone could grasp about these matters could be carried in my words, than set down my own meaning so plainly that it shut out every other reading which, not being false, could not offend me. So I will not be so rash, my God, as to disbelieve that you granted at least as much to that great man. Without a doubt, when he wrote those words, he perceived and had in mind whatever truth we have managed to find in them, and indeed whatever truth we have not managed to find, and still have not, but which may yet be found there.

Finally, Lord, you who are God and not flesh and blood — if a mere man saw less, could anything be hidden from your good Spirit (who will lead me into the land of uprightness), which you yourself intended, through those words, to reveal to readers in times to come, even though the one through whom they were spoken perhaps had only one meaning in mind among many true ones? And if that is so, let whatever he had in mind be, of all the readings, the highest. But to us, Lord, either reveal that same meaning, or any other true one you please — so that, whether you uncover for us the very meaning you gave to your servant, or some other meaning by occasion of those words, you may still feed us, and not let error deceive us. See, Lord my God, how much we have written about a few words — how much, I beg you! What strength of ours, or how many ages, would be enough to treat all your books this way? Allow me, then, in what remains, to confess to you more briefly, and to choose some one true, certain, and good sense that you inspire in me — even though many readings may present themselves, where many may indeed be found. Let this be the law of my confession: that if I say what your minister intended, that is right and best; that is what I should aim for — and if I do not reach it, I should at least say what your Truth wanted to tell me by his words, the same Truth that also revealed to him what it wanted.
